title: The Laboratory Cyrus Poonawalla Put in a Corner of the Stud Farm
dek: In 1966, with horse racing in decline, a Pune horse breeder took a vet's suggestion and began making tetanus antitoxin on the family farm.

story.event: Setting up a laboratory on the family stud farm to make tetanus antitoxin
story.summary: In 1966 Cyrus Poonawalla, seeing little future in his family's horse-breeding business, acted on a vet's suggestion and set up a small laboratory on the Poonawalla stud farm near Pune to make tetanus antitoxin from horse serum, with scientists recruited from the government's Haffkine Institute. Production began in 1967; by 1974 the Serum Institute of India also made tetanus and DTP vaccines, and it later became the world's largest vaccine maker by doses.
paragraphs: In 1966, on the day Cyrus Poonawalla married, the foundation stone was laid for a small laboratory in a corner of his family's stud farm near Pune. It was a small-scale unit with capital of about five lakh rupees, and Poonawalla later admitted to the writer Coomi Kapoor that its name, the Serum Institute of India, overstated both its size and its standing at the time.

His father, Soli, had founded the stud farm in 1946. After a commerce degree in 1962, Cyrus saw little future in it, Kapoor writes, because Bombay State's chief minister, Morarji Desai, had banned horse racing. In a socialist India, he told BioSpectrum in 2004, the "King of Sports" had no future as "an economically viable business career". He built a prototype sports car modelled on a Jaguar, then dropped it as too ambitious.

The idea came from the farm's consulting vet, Dr Balakrishnan. The Poonawallas had been giving horses to the government's Haffkine Institute in Bombay, where they were used to make tetanus antiserum. Why not, he suggested, make the antitoxin, and anti-snake-venom serum too, on the farm itself? Both were scarce in India. The family had horses and spare land. Through the family doctor, Jal Mehta, Poonawalla reached P. M. Wagle, recently retired as Haffkine's director, and hired scientists who knew the work.

The harder part was the state. Permission to build, electricity and a drug licence "all were new to us", he said, and he began "with little in my pocket". With fewer than 20 staff, the laboratory started making tetanus antitoxin in late 1967; once it was on sale in 1968, he said, banks would lend. By 1974 the institute also made a tetanus vaccine and the combined diphtheria, tetanus and whooping-cough vaccine. Poonawalla said it paid no dividends for about thirty years, ploughing profits back.
In time it stopped drawing serum from horses and turned to discarded army mules. It grew into the world's largest vaccine maker by number of doses, while the stud farm kept breeding racehorses.

quote.text: But the Marquis of Worcester, Watt, and Fulton bethought themselves, that, where was power, was not devil, but was God; that it must be availed of, and not by any means let off and wasted.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Emerson praises the engineers who looked at the steam everyone vented through a hole in the lid and saw work it could do. Poonawalla called his raw material "discarded resources of plasma"; the turn came from someone pointing out what was already leaving the farm.

reflection: The future Poonawalla wanted, horses and fast cars, was closing, and the one that opened was not his idea. A vet who knew the farm saw that what it already produced, and gave away, was needed elsewhere. Poonawalla's part was to listen, then to find people who knew the science he did not.
When a plan you love stops working, it is tempting to look far away for the next one. It may be worth asking the people who know your work well what they see you giving away without noticing.
invitation: Ask one colleague who has watched you work for a while what they think you do, or have, that is undervalued. Write their answer down without arguing with it.

research_notes: Starting capital: Poonawalla told BioSpectrum (2004) 'around Rs five lakh or even less than that', and Coomi Kapoor (2021) and The Asian Age (2019) give five lakh; Asterisk (2025) says he invested Rs 99,000 ($12,000), and Bloomberg and Quartz profiles say he raised $12,000 by selling horses and borrowed the rest from his father. The story uses the founder's and Kapoor's figure of about five lakh. Origin of the idea: popular accounts say Poonawalla himself realised he could make serum instead of donating horses to Haffkine; his own account to BioSpectrum and Kapoor's both credit the farm's vet, Dr Balakrishnan, and the story follows them. Age: BioSpectrum and The Asian Age (quoting him) say he started at 22, but Asterisk gives his birth year as 1941, which would make him about 25; the story gives no age. His brother is spelled Zavary in BioSpectrum and Zavere in Kapoor; the story does not name him. Dates: 1966 is the founding (foundation stone, per Kapoor; 'unit was born in 1966', per Poonawalla); manufacturing began in late 1967 and the first product went on sale in 1968, per Poonawalla. The racing ban is attributed to Kapoor (Asterisk also mentions it); Poonawalla himself framed it as racing having no viable future in socialist India. P. M. Wagle is named by Kapoor; BioSpectrum mentions only 'a retired director of Haffkine Institute'. The Quartz profile (403) and Bloomberg profile were not used as sources. The Emerson passage is about steam engineers, applied here by analogy; 'discarded resources of plasma' is Poonawalla's phrase in BioSpectrum.
